title: Comparing
goal: Describe things and people, compare them, and accept the agreement that binds the whole of Finnish together: an adjective always takes the same form as its noun.
bekal: make adjectives agree with their noun in every ending you've learned

dialogs.title: Dialog — Kumpi on parempi?
dialogs.intro: Budi is looking for a second-hand bike. Marek helps him look at two options advertised online.

lines.speaker: Marek:
lines.text: Katso näitä kahta pyörää. Kumpi on parempi?
lines.id: Look at these two bikes. Which one is better?
lines.literal: look these-part two-part bike-part. which-of-two is better?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Tämä musta on uudempi, mutta se on kalliimpi.
lines.id: This black one is newer, but it's more expensive.
lines.literal: this black is newer, but it is more-expensive.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: A hundred euros. The older one costs eighty.

lines.speaker: Marek:
lines.text: Halvempi on hyvä valinta, jos se toimii.
lines.id: The cheaper one is a good choice, if it works.
lines.literal: cheaper is good choice, if it works.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: But the old bike has rust on it.

lines.speaker: Marek:
lines.text: Ruoste ei ole pahin ongelma. Jarrut ovat tärkeämmät.
lines.id: Rust isn't the worst problem. The brakes matter more.
lines.literal: rust not is worst problem. brakes are more-important.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Totta. Suomessa talvi on pisin vuodenaika.
lines.id: True. In Finland winter is the longest season.
lines.literal: true. in-Finland winter is longest season.

lines.speaker: Marek:
lines.text: Ja liukkain! Osta se kalliimpi, mutta turvallisempi.
lines.id: And the most slippery! Buy the more expensive but safer one.
lines.literal: and most-slippery! buy that more-expensive, but safer.

lines.speaker: Marek:
lines.text: Ei, minä olen vain vanhempi. Se on eri asia.
lines.id: No, I'm just older. That's a different thing.
lines.literal: no, I am only older. it is different thing.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Paras vastaus tänään. Ostan sen mustan.
lines.id: Best answer today. I'll buy the black one.
lines.literal: best answer today. buy-I that-whole black-whole.

notes: **Vanhassa pyörässä** — the adjective takes the same ending as its noun. This agreement holds for **every** ending without exception: *iso talo → isossa talossa → isolle talolle → isot talot*. Once you've got it, it never catches you out again, because there isn't a single exception.

**Kalliimpi, halvempi, uudempi** — the "more" ending is **-mpi**. Note that the last vowel of the base word often changes to *-e-* or lengthens: *halpa → halve**mpi***, *kallis → kallii**mpi***, *uusi → uude**mpi***.

**Parempi and paras are irregular.** *Hyvä* (good) → *parempi* (better) → *paras* (best). It's the only truly rebellious Finnish adjective, and also one of the most used. Just like English *good/better/best* — the same irregular pattern.
**Kuin = than.** *Viisaampi **kuin** minä*. The word being compared stays in its basic form, untouched. This is the easiest way and completely correct; there's a more compact way, but it's beyond A1.

**Pisin, liukkain, pahin** — the "most" ending is **-in**, and it often shortens the base word: *pitkä → pisin*, *liukas → liukkain*, *paha → pahin*. Superlatives can't always be guessed, so learn them together with the base word.
**Tärkeämmät, with a plural ending.** The "more" form still agrees with its noun: *jarrut ovat tärkeä**mmät***. Even comparison doesn't escape agreement.

grammars.title: Adjectives always copy their noun
body: One rule, no exceptions: whatever ending the noun takes, the adjective takes the same one. Finnish is far tidier here than German or French, with their tables of exceptions.
after: The practice is simple: every time you put an ending on a noun, say the adjective first with the same ending. Before long your hand writes it on its own.
⚠️ Gradation still applies to each word separately: *iso**lla** pöydä**llä*** — *pöytä* weakens to *pöydä-*, while *iso* has no k/p/t to weaken.
Demonstratives (*tämä*, *tuo*, *se*) join in too: *tässä isossa talossa*, *sen mustan pyörän*. Once the pattern sinks in, the whole phrase moves together like a single word.

grammars.title: More and most
body: Two endings: **-mpi** for "more", **-in** for "most". What needs attention is how the base word changes.
after: **Comparing two things:** *A on isompi **kuin** B.* — *Helsinki on isompi kuin Tampere.* The word after *kuin* doesn't change form at all.
**Naming the best:** *Tämä on **paras** kahvila Helsingissä.* The superlative stands before its noun like any adjective, and takes its ending too: *parhaassa kahvilassa*.
⚠️ *Paljon* and *vähän* have completely different comparative forms (*enemmän*, *vähemmän*), and both are very common: *Haluan enemmän kahvia*, *Puhun vähemmän kuin ennen*.

blocks.text: Learning adjectives in pairs is much faster than one by one, because memory stores them as one thing, not two. The same trick works for prepositions and verbs of motion.

⚠️ Calling someone **hiljainen** (quiet) isn't a criticism in Finland — it's often a compliment. On the other hand, *puhelias* can sound slightly accusing, depending on the tone. The social scale runs the opposite way from many cultures, and it's one of the cultural differences that confuses newcomers most.

blocks.title: Describing without offending
items: *Hän on tosi mukava.* — He's/She's really nice.
*Hän on vähän hiljainen, mutta ystävällinen.* — He's/She's a bit quiet, but kind.
Commenting on someone's looks — weight, height, age — feels much more personal in Finland than in many places. Safe: character and actions. Not safe: bodies.

exercises.prompt: Make the adjective agree with its noun.

items: This one is newer but more expensive.
This is the best café in Helsinki.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.

answers: isompi, isoin — pienempi, pienin — kalliimpi, kallein — halvempi, halvin — parempi, paras — vaikeampi, vaikein
